title: Fatima, 1917
hook: three shepherd children and a call to prayer and penance

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles de Foucauld, the soldier who became the universal brother to the Tuareg. Your line was brother to everyone. Did you learn a word in someone else's language? Today, shepherd children, and a jail cell. Day nine hundred three.

A town official in Portugal loads some children into his carriage. They are shepherds from the hamlet of Aljustrel, near Fatima: Lucia and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta. For months they have said that a lady from heaven appears to them on the thirteenth of each month, and crowds now follow them to the field. The official is not a believer, and his government is suspicious of the Church. He wants the crowds gone and the children's secret out. Instead of taking them to the field, he takes them to his town and locks them up.
screen: `A CARRIAGE, A TOWN OFFICIAL.` → `CROWDS IN A FIELD.` → `CHILDREN LOCKED UP.`

segments.voice: Stay with those few days, from the field to the cell. First, the message. The children said the lady asked them to pray the rosary every day for peace and for the end of the war, and to do penance, small sacrifices offered for others. Europe was at war, and Portuguese soldiers were in it. Second, the pressure. In Lucia's later memoirs, the official questioned them, and when they refused to tell what the lady had confided to them, he threatened them with death. They were frightened. They still wouldn't tell. Third, the cell. Lucia recalled that the children were put in a room with the town's prisoners. Jacinta was crying for her mother. Then the children knelt and began to pray the rosary, and some of the prisoners knelt and prayed with them. Grown men in a jail, following children through the Hail Mary. Fourth, the outcome. The children were sent home, and they said the lady came to them again a few days later, in a different spot. In the end the Church judged the appearances worthy of belief; Catholics are free to accept or not, since the Church calls such events private revelations. At its center is a prayer older than Fatima: the angel's words in the Gospel of Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." This week ran through a freed slave, an heiress, an immigrant, a little book, children at the altar, a desert brother, and now children praying in a jail.
screen: `THE ROSARY, FOR PEACE.` · `THREATENED, AND SILENT.` · `PRISONERS KNEEL WITH CHILDREN.` · `WORTHY OF BELIEF, NOT REQUIRED.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the rosary for peace. Two minutes won't hold a whole rosary, so take a small piece. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place at war right now. If you pray, you can say the Hail Mary slowly, once or a few times, for the people there, using beads or your fingers. If you don't pray, hold that place in silence, and wish its people safety and an end to the fighting. The children prayed in a frightening place; a prayer for peace can start anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Fatima. A village in Portugal where, the children said, a lady asked for the rosary, penance, and prayer for peace.
Your line: pray for peace. Today, read one news story about a war, all the way through, and then name its people in a prayer or in silence. Day nine hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Our Lady of Fatima on 13 May; pilgrims go to the shrine at Fatima, and in parishes people pray the rosary together, often adding a prayer for peace.

trapdoor: what you thought: Fatima is a story about a miracle in the sky.
what it means: a call to the rosary, penance and prayer for peace, carried by children under pressure.
what a scholar hears: Lucia's memoirs describe the jailing, and the Church treats Fatima as a private revelation, approved but not required.

notes: Week end (days 897–903): look-back at the end of the teach.
Year-two day 668 covered the Fatima story overall, the sun, and private revelation as its myth; this day takes the August jailing at Ourém as its angle to avoid repetition.

Jailing details (taken by the administrator of Ourém, Artur de Oliveira Santos; threatened with death, tradition says by boiling oil; put with prisoners; rosary prayed; prisoners joining; Jacinta crying for her mother) follow Lucia's memoirs; confirm.
'His government is suspicious of the Church' (the anticlerical First Republic): confirm wording.
Later appearance 'a few days later, in a different spot' refers to Valinhos (19 August); confirm.
Claims rule: no ages, no crowd size, and no approval year given. 'Portuguese soldiers were in it' (Portugal in the First World War): confirm.
CCC 67 on private revelation: confirm citation.
Editor pass: 'a jail full of grown men' overstated Lucia's account (some prisoners joined); now 'grown men in a jail'.

Second editor pass: teach opener 'Fatima turns four ways here' replaced (template repeated across the week); the third myth item, which the script never set up ('the children were the only ones who wanted the crowds gone'), replaced with one the hook answers (the official took them to his town, not the field).
